do: Ensure every interactive element (links, buttons, form controls, custom widgets) has a clearly visible focus indicator when receiving keyboard focus.
Use CSS pseudo-classes (:focus and :focus-visible) to provide strong and clearly perceivable outlines or styles.
Provide focus indicators with sufficient color contrast against adjacent backgrounds (minimum 3:1).
Ensure custom focus indicators are at least as visible as the default user agent focus outline.
Maintain or enhance the browser's default focus styles if custom styles are applied.
Use consistent focus styles across the website or application for predictability.
Design focus indicators with enough padding, glow, or border thickness to be distinguishable.
Ensure focus indicators remain visible regardless of scrolling, sticky headers, or fixed containers.
Confirm that focus indicators do not get cut off by overflow clipping, transforms, or container styling.
Test keyboard navigation thoroughly using Tab, Shift+Tab, and arrow keys to ensure focus is always visible.
Check focus visibility in light and dark themes, and under high-contrast or forced-color modes.
Provide consistent focus styles across the site or application for predictability.
Use techniques such as thick outlines, background highlights, or underline changes for better visibility.
For custom components, use JavaScript to manage and expose focus states properly.
Test focus visibility at different zoom levels and in OS/browser high contrast modes.
dont: Don’t remove default browser focus styles (outline: none) without providing a visible, accessible alternative.
Don’t rely solely on subtle visual changes (e.g., small color shifts) that may be imperceptible to low-vision users.
Don’t create focus indicators that disappear against backgrounds with insufficient contrast.
Don’t design custom widgets (e.g., carousels, modals, dropdowns) without visible focus states.
Don’t override focus styles in a way that makes them thinner, faint, or less visible than default styles.
Don’t rely only on hover styles to signal interactivity; focus must be clearly distinguishable from hover.
Don’t hide or clip focus indicators using overflow: hidden, transforms, or clipping regions.
Don’t rely on transparent or off-screen outlines as a replacement for a visible indicator.
Don’t depend solely on color to indicate focus — use additional visual cues like shape, border, or thickness.
Don’t move focus unexpectedly with JavaScript without informing the user.
Don’t apply focus styles only for hover states — keyboard focus must always be handled separately.
edge_cases: Custom JavaScript components may not inherit default focus styles if tabindex or ARIA roles are misused.
Low-contrast hover/focus schemes may look acceptable to designers but fail for users with low vision.
Single-page applications may temporarily lose visible focus indicators when routes change or elements re-render.
Sticky or fixed-position elements can push focus indicators off-screen during scrolling.
Touch-device hybrid interactions may cause developers to disable focus outlines incorrectly, harming keyboard users.
High-contrast or forced-color modes may override or hide custom focus styles; ensure indicators remain perceivable.
For non-native controls built with <div> or <span>, developers must add custom focus styles explicitly.
Focus indicators may be lost if CSS frameworks reset or override browser defaults without accessible replacements.
Using complex CSS (clip-path, transform, overflow-hidden) may unintentionally hide focus outlines.
Some browsers apply different focus behaviors (e.g., Chrome uses :focus-visible, Safari uses :focus), so cross-browser testing is necessary.
Third-party widgets or embedded components (iframes) may not expose visible focus correctly.
Keyboard focus indicators are removed or have insufficient visual contrast.
Focus outline is visible only in certain color themes or disappears during animation.
Focus indicators appear off-screen or are hidden by other interface elements.
Users navigating by keyboard cannot visually track their position.
Automation detects CSS focus styles but cannot assess actual visibility for human users.
Focus visibility issues on specific element types (logos, custom buttons).
Dynamic focus states that change visibility based on user interaction.
